name: Crowned Ladies NW
_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading. The heading names the
network these frames are cut FOR and the channel is the show they are
cut from, so another show cutting for the same network is one more
folder under it rather than a heading of its own.
Like every channel under this heading it is a frame fetcher rather
than a thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of
vertical stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said
over it.
It is cut to Hall of Femme's design, and that pack is the one to read
first: the frame fetch, the 540x960 vertical output, the
transcription, the rewrite, the card at the foot of the frame, the
palette handed to the user, the highlight that changes FACE and not
colour - all of it is Hall of Femme's and is named here rather than
restated. What makes this show itself is one sentence long: it is set
in Cormorant Garamond with picked words in Great Vibes, on a plum
card, in a champagne the user can swap for the card's own colour. The
casing is the one further thing it changes, and it changes it because
the faces leave it no choice - see `uppercase` below.
The NW in the name is the account's, the way the FR is in Crowned
Ladies FR and the DE in Hall of Femme DE: it says which of the brand's
feeds this is and not what language the app is in. What lands on the
frames is whatever the video's own voice track was saying, put through
the transcription and the rewrite exactly as on every channel here,
and everything the app itself says is English like the rest of it (see
CLAUDE.md).
It shares a brand with Crowned Ladies FR and shares no design with it,
which is worth saying out loud because the two folders sort next to
each other and somebody will assume one was copied from the other.
That feed is Helvetica, one magenta, no card and no highlight, set
straight onto the photograph. This one was cut from Hall of Femme
instead, on the instruction that it follow that pack: it keeps the
card, keeps the palette and keeps the two-face highlight. They are two
accounts of one brand and not two colourways of one pack, and a change
to either is not a change to the other.
The id is kebab-case ASCII because it is also the folder name and the
key everything else refers to; the name is the brand.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.
_comment_title: Where this show parts company with the pack it was cut from, which is
in the type and in the two colours and nowhere else. Hall of Femme
sets its captions in Telegraf - a 200-weight hairline for the block,
the 800 for a picked word - on a hot pink card, in sixteen pairings
the user chooses between. This one is set in Cormorant Garamond with
picked words in Great Vibes, on a plum card, in four pairings of that
plum and a champagne.
Everything else - the size, where the lines break, the freeform text
box, the shape of the card, its padding and corners and shadow, where
the block stands on the frame, the drag - is the Snapchat caption
design and is stated once, in content/presets/snapchat-caption.json.
This pack states what makes it this show, and then states the one key
the faces force it to override.
The pairing is the idea. A Garamond and a copperplate script are what
an invitation is set in, and they are drawn to sit together: the serif
carries the sentence and the script is what a name or a title is
written in. That is the same division of labour Hall of Femme gets out
of one family's two ends, arrived at with two different kinds of
writing instead of two weights - see `highlight`.
Both faces are light, and on this heading that is normally the
argument for a card (Hall of Femme's own note makes it: a hairline
over an unknown photograph is the one thing a caption must never be).
The card is kept here for exactly that reason and not merely because
the pack it was copied from had one - a high-contrast serif has thins
that go to nothing over a blown-out still, and a joined script has
hairline joins that go first.

_comment_face: Cormorant Garamond Regular. Which cut of the family that is, why
the full name rather than 'Cormorant Garamond' is declared, and
what happens when the file is missing are all written out in
One consequence of the face reaches this pack, and it is worth
knowing before anybody changes the casing back. A Garamond has a
small lower case relative to its capitals - 386 units of the em
against 625 - so at the preset's stated 40px the x-height is 15.4px
where Hall of Femme's Telegraf gives 20.0px. Set in lower case, a
caption here reads a little smaller than the same caption on its
That is accepted rather than corrected. `fontSize` is 40 on every
channel under this heading and no pack has ever overridden it: the
preset's argument is that burned-in speech is ONE size, always, and
a pack that nudged it because its own face is delicate would be the
first crack in that. The capitals lose almost nothing by comparison
- 25.0px against 26.6px - so what the size costs is a consequence of
the casing below and not of the size.
_comment_uppercase: Off, and this is the one guideline of Hall of Femme's that this
pack breaks. It is the third channel under the heading to break it
- Killer Bites and Re-belle are the others, and Re-belle's note is
the one to read beside this, because the reason is the same reason
arriving from a different direction.
The preset's argument for capitals is that at 40px with twenty
characters to a line a caption is three short beats rather than a
paragraph, and beats are what capitals are for. That argument is
about grotesques. Neither face here is one, and the highlight face
is the one that settles it: Great Vibes is a copperplate script,
and a copperplate script has no capitals in the sense the preset
means. Its letters are drawn to JOIN, and the joins live in the
lower case. Set in capitals it comes apart into a row of
unconnected swash initials - not a louder version of the same hand
but a different and far harder object to read.
It is measurably worse as well as visually worse, which is why this
is not a matter of taste. Great Vibes' capitals are 44% wider than
Cormorant's for the same string, and they reach 34.4px above the
baseline and 16.0px below at 40px against its lower case's 25.2 and
14.0. A picked word in capitals would therefore be both the widest
thing on its line by a long way and the thing that sets the height
of every card in the block - two words swelling a caption in both
directions, which is the opposite of what picking a word out is
supposed to do.
The block's own face agrees for a quieter reason. A Garamond's
lower case is the half of it anyone recognises - the long
ascenders, the small round bowls, the descenders that hang - and set
in capitals it becomes a perfectly good inscriptional serif that
could be any of fifty others. The face was chosen for what it is;
capitals would spend it.
It is applied at the draw and not to what is stored, so turning it
off changes only what the canvas does: the text box held the user's
own casing all along, and the highlight buttons already offered the
words as the canvas would set them (see the `cased` note in
js/text.js and editor.renderWordButtons).
`uppercase` is the block's and there is one of it, so this reaches
the picked words too. That is the answer both faces wanted, which is
the whole of why it can be one key.
_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set in
until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of its
own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to (see
state.textColorFor). It is one of the two in `colors` below, so the
champagne swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an untouched
frame.
Champagne letters on the plum card is the pairing this show opens
on, and with a palette of two the only decision here is which of
them is the CARD. It opened the other way round - plum type on a
champagne card - on the argument that the card is a fifth of the
frame and a shape that size in the plum is a dark slab over the
picture the stills exist to show. That is still true and it is no
longer the answer: this is the brand colour, and on a heading where
every other show puts its colour on the card, a caption that carried
it only in the letters read as the pale card belonging to nobody.
The slab is the plum and the type is the champagne on it.
Contrast is unchanged by the swap, which is what makes it free:
9.6 to 1 either way round, the widest margin any pack under this
heading carries and what a high-contrast serif with thin strokes
actually needs. What the swap does cost is the picture - a dark card
covers more of the still than a pale one appears to - and the
preset's shadow stops earning its keep, since it was written to
survive a pale slab thrown onto a pale wall and now falls from a
dark one. Neither is worth a number of this pack's own: the shadow
is the Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in the preset.
The other three pairings are a button away, the inverse among them.
_comment_colors: The two colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and for
the card behind them - two buttons each in the title panel (see
editor.renderColorButtons).
The same two in both lists and in one order, which is what every
pack under this heading does and for their reason: the point is the
PAIRING. Four combinations of a plum and a champagne, and the two
worth having are the two that read. A palette that could only ever
be used one way round would be a palette of one card, and this
show's look is the pairing rather than either colour on its own.
Two colours rather than the four Hall of Femme offers, and that is
the brand and not an unfinished list - the two that were asked for
are the two the show has. Nothing counts these entries - the panel
draws a swatch per colour and the row wraps - so a third is one
string in this file the day the show has one.
Nothing stops the user setting plum on plum. That is not an
oversight either: the two lists are independent because the pairing
is the feature, and with a palette this short a rule barring the two
matching combinations would be a rule removing half the buttons. The
user can see the caption has gone and presses the other swatch.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block - see the note on
`colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a different
FACE and not a different colour, so what colour the type is has one
answer and not two. That matters more on a palette of two than on
one of four: with the block in champagne, a highlight left to pick
its own colour from the same list could only ever be plum, and plum
on plum is a picked word that vanishes into its card.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Great Vibes, in the same colour as the rest
of the block. The highlight here is the KIND OF WRITING: a Garamond
and a copperplate script on one line, which is the pairing an
invitation has used for three hundred years - the sentence is
typeset and the name in it is written.
It is Hall of Femme's highlight with the technique swapped. That
pack picks words out by weight, 200 against 800 of one family, on
the argument that at that contrast it is as loud as a box would be
and leaves the card one clean shape instead of a shape with a second
shape inside it. Both halves of that argument survive the swap: a
script in the middle of a serif is at least as loud as two weights
of one family, and it costs the card nothing.
The colour it names is the block's, so the recolour draws exactly
what its neighbours are drawn in and the face is the whole of the
difference. Stated all the same, for the fallback reason `color`
above is stated, and because a highlight that changed colour as well
as hand would be two highlights.
The mode and the scope come from the preset, which is where the
argument for picking out words rather than lines lives - and it is
an argument this channel depends on more than most. What a script is
FOR is a word: a name, a place, the thing the clip turns on. A whole
line of it would be handwriting pretending to be a caption.
One consequence is worth knowing before picking many words at once.
Every box in the block takes one shared vertical band, and the band
is the union of what every row needs (see js/text.js), so a row
carrying a Great Vibes word makes every card in the caption as tall
as that word's ascenders and descenders ask for - about 43px at 40px
against the 27px a row of Telegraf capitals asks for on Hall of
Femme. A four-line caption here is therefore a visibly taller stack
than the same caption there. It is still inside the frame with room
to spare, since the block stands on the preset's 120px margin and
grows upward from it, and `maxBlockHeightRatio` does not pull it in:
at a stated `fontSize` there is no size left to shrink, which the
preset says where it states the size.
No shadow stated, so the preset's null stands: these letters are on
a solid card in a colour the user picked, and the card casts the one
shadow there is. A drop shadow under a script this fine would smear
the joins that make it a script.
_comment_panel: Plum, and the fill is the one thing about the card this pack
decides: its shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow are the
Snapchat caption design and come from the preset.
It is the first entry in `colors.panel` above and the type is the
second, which is the freedom Hall of Femme's note points out: the
swatch that shows as chosen is found by matching this value and not
by being listed first, so both rows stay written in one order
whichever way round the show opens.
The preset's shadow is half opaque and falls straight down, and its
note argues it from the hardest case a card can face - a white slab
thrown onto a white wall. A plum card is not that case and the
shadow does less here than it does next door. It is kept without a
number of this pack's own, because a card that casts no shadow at
all is a card printed on the photograph rather than lying on it,
and because the fill is the one thing about this card that is the

_comment_branding: No dark gradient. It exists to hold a title legible against the
photograph, and this title is not against the photograph at all - it
is on a card of its own. A scrim over every still would darken forty
pictures to solve a problem the card has already solved.
There is a second reason here that its hot pink parent does not have.
This card is pale and the type on it is dark, so a gradient behind the
card would change nothing about the caption and would only darken the
picture the card already covers a fifth of.
